earlier_context.quote: The second kind is *homilies*, which we call a “word,” and they are delivered to the people. The third kind is *tomes*, which we call books or volumes. Homilies are for the common people; tomes, that is, books, are of a more substantial disputation. A dialogue is a conference of two persons, from *dia* and *logos*, which is “the speech of two.” A treatise is the manifold exposition of a single subject. Commentaries are so called as if “comments”; for they are interpretations: comments on law, comments on the Gospel. An apologetic is a book of excuse, in which certain persons are accustomed to answer accusers. A panegyric, that is, laudatory, is a licentious and wanton kind of speaking, in praises of kings and princes; in composing it men flatter with many lies. A prologue is a preface before a book, as the prologue of blessed Jerome on Genesis. A proem is the beginning of a speech or work, and is often taken for a preface. A *simperasma* is the conclusion of some work, and in our usage it is treated as of the third declension, like *dogma*. *Biblos*, that is, a codex, is a book of many books, as the codex of the Bible, which contains many books. A book is a partial treatise divided by itself, or a single one, as one book of Augustine on penance, or four on Christian doctrine, etc. A volume is a book, so called from rolling, as volumes of the law, volumes of the prophets.
